subject: Beta estimates, X2 and p values are the same for SIBTEST and CSIBTEST

messages.author: 43d8e5920c5b5dac
messages.subject: Beta estimates, X2 and p values are the same for SIBTEST and CSIBTEST
parts:
Hello Phil,

I am testing uniform and nonuniform DIF for a set of polytomous items. I have a couple of questions:

1) I noticed that with the exception of 1 item, the absolute values of the Beta estimates, X2 and p values are exactly the same for SIBTEST and CSIBTEST.  Is this something expected?

2) Why are SEs not estimated (reported as NA)  for CSIBTEST beta values. 

3) Negative beta estimates indicate item favoring the focal group in SIBTEST. Am I correct?


Many thanks!

messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: Beta estimates, X2 and p values are the same for SIBTEST and CSIBTEST
parts:
On Sun, Oct 28, 2018 at 11:21 PM eaez <eay...@fordham.edu> wrote:
Hello Phil,

I am testing uniform and nonuniform DIF for a set of polytomous items. I have a couple of questions:

1) I noticed that with the exception of 1 item, the absolute values of the Beta estimates, X2 and p values are exactly the same for SIBTEST and CSIBTEST.  Is this something expected?
Yes. When no crossing location is detected within the range of the total scores then CSIBTEST reduces exactly to SIBTEST.
2) Why are SEs not estimated (reported as NA)  for CSIBTEST beta values.
It's significance is based on the sum of two chi^2 components, so the SEs are not as straightforward.
3) Negative beta estimates indicate item favoring the focal group in SIBTEST. Am I correct?

Correct.
 


Many thanks!

I`d appreciate any guidance on this.

Thanks again!

messages.subject: Re: Beta estimates, X2 and p values are the same for SIBTEST and CSIBTEST
parts:
On Mon, Oct 29, 2018 at 12:22 AM eaez <eay...@fordham.edu> wrote:
Thank you!

To follow up on this, do you recommend significance testing results (with or without p-value correction for repeated testing) or the magnitude of beta estimates to identify items with DIF?

I found some previous work uses some criteria to categorize small (<= .05), medium (between 0.05 and 0.1) and large (>.1) DIF based on beta values; however such categorization does not always agree with significance test results. I`d appreciate any guidance on this.

Sure, these are purely sample size specific though. It's entirely possible to obtain a large beta which is non-significant without sufficient information to reject the null hypothesis. With larger sample sizes, whereby the certainly of the betas is better due to reduced sampling variability, then your betas would stabilize and you'd reach the correct conclusions from both lines of reasoning. You might think of p-values as a litmus test at minimum, where if you can't reject the null then there's a good chance you shouldn't interpret the magnitude of the beta either. 

Phil

Thanks again!
